extracted.intended_audience: researchers, theoreticians, and informed readers evaluating claimed P vs. NP proofs (TCS/mathematics community and interested public)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating claimed P vs NP proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community-discussed criteria for judging the correctness, significance, and value of claimed proofs (especially high-profile claims like P vs NP). Covers technical checks, exposition/versioning practices, and signals of lasting value even if the proof fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evade known barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must prove how his proof evades the known barriers (relativization, natural proofs and algebrization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly demonstrate why the approach is not ruled out by standard barrier results; reviewers should check whether the paper addresses these specific obstacles. (Suggested addition in comment #48.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use of locality and techniques for complex fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical arguments that rely on locality or techniques to deal with complex fixed points must be used correctly and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the three issues raised in response to Deolalikar's paper was '(a) the use of locality and the techniques used to deal with complex fixed points' — authors should clarify and defend these uses in revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate problem variants properly (e.g., 9-SAT vs XORSAT/2-SAT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must correctly account for differences between problem variants (for example, between 9-SAT and XORSAT/2-SAT) when reducing or arguing about hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusing distinct problem types or treating them interchangeably is a technical error; reviewers flagged the 9-SAT vs XORSAT/2-SAT distinction as a substantive issue to be clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify parametrization methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of parametrization used in the proof must be clearly explained and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the raised issues was '(c) clarification on the method of parametrization.' Authors should add explicit definitions, parameter choices, and why they are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make correct claims about computational models and complexity (bit-length vs real models, exact vs approximate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about membership in P/NP and complexity of algorithms must respect the appropriate computational model (bit-length/bit-model vs real/BSS model) and distinguish exact vs approximate solvability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As noted in the SDP discussion: semidefinite programming is only approximately (weak-membership and ϵ-optimality) solvable in polynomial time; exact membership/optimum issues depend on the model. Authors should not hand-wave such distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address reviewers' technical objections in revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When issues are raised (by blog commenters or referees), revisions should explicitly address them rather than leaving the paper a 'moving target'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stated they would address the three issues in the version being prepared. Good practice: list raised objections and how each was fixed, ideally in changelog or revision notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post stable, public versions (e.g., arXiv) so the paper isn't a moving target
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should post versions (for example, on the arXiv) to avoid the paper being a moving target and to make it possible for commentators to reference fixed texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greg Kuperberg suggested posting versions to the arXiv; this aids transparent community scrutiny and citation of particular versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek expert consultation before wide public release
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors (especially those venturing outside their main area) should consult domain experts before publicizing high-profile claims to avoid mistakes due to lack of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments point out it's easy for an expert in one area to err in another; pre-release consultation can prevent elementary but damaging errors and reduce noise in public discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit for formal peer/journal review (and be clear what 'peer' means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond public commentary, authors should send the paper for formal peer and journal review; if claiming 'peer' review via internet, clarify what that entails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author mentioned sending a version 'for peer and journal review' and a commenter asked '"peer" = internet?' — be explicit about the review process used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition and purpose-specific reading
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be written so readers can accomplish different purposes (verify correctness, understand high-level ideas, adapt/generalize, assess novelty); exposition should support those aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott notes that reading differs by purpose (verify correctness vs understanding vs novelty assessment). Good expository practices: clear structure, stated goals, key lemmas highlighted, and intuitive explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide understanding, not just a correctness certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians value proofs that provide human understanding; a contribution that increases conceptual understanding can be valuable even if the proof is ultimately flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terry Tao (via Thurston) is cited: 'mathematicians ultimately are not after proofs; they are after understanding.' Value can accrue from insights and new viewpoints generated by the attempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and cleverness of approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof approach that introduces a move or idea not previously considered (even if ultimately insufficient) is a positive signal of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tim Gowers noted Deolalikar 'is making a move that I, for one, had not thought of.' Novel but well-motivated ideas deserve attention and can seed further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community impact / stimulates productive research
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed proof has enduring value if it stimulates top researchers to work on new obstructions, generates fruitful discussion, or otherwise advances the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Sidles' 'Six Signs A Claimed P≠NP Proof Is Valuable' includes endorsements/interest by notable researchers, clever elementary approaches, program-story value, and the strategy not being dismissed outright. Impact can be measured by subsequent research and discussion it produces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest handling of corrections and iterative improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should acknowledge errors, publish errata or corrected versions, and transparently document fixes rather than obfuscating or denying problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meta-proof excerpt and comments emphasize that iterative corrections are normal; transparency about what changed helps reviewers follow progress and reduces confusion.
